title: Token slab SIMD bridge and adaptive cache eviction for prefill hot lanes
creator: Asha Patel
description:
Problem: Current prefill-side preprocessing spends disproportionate CPU cycles on byte-level normalization and UTF8 reassembly for short prompts that dominate PLG traffic. Existing token cache eviction is LRU across sessions which causes repeated re-ingest of common prefixes under memory pressure.

Proposal: Implement a 'token slab' in-memory layout optimized for SIMD-friendly ingestion plus a lightweight bridge that transforms normalized input directly into slab-aligned token batches. Complement this with an adaptive eviction policy (hot-slab bias + frequency decay) tuned for short-session PLG workloads so frequently reused prompt prefixes remain resident.

Goals:
- Reduce per-request preprocessing CPU by 30% on short (<=256 token) prompts.
- Reduce end-to-end prefill latency 95p by 15ms on p50/p95 workloads in hosted mode.
- Keep additional memory overhead under 12% on 32GB host machines.

Scope and deliverables:
- New in-memory 'token slab' representation and allocator (C++ runtime) with alignment for AVX2/AVX512 loads.
- SIMD bridge that performs normalization, small-chunk segmentation, and mapping to slab indices with minimal branching.
- Adaptive eviction policy: combine a hot-slab score (recency+frequency) with a decay multiplier tuned by workload telemetry.
- Integration tests, microbenchmarks, and a canary against canary-hosting region.
- Dashboard panels for slab hit-rate, preprocessing CPU, and eviction churn.

Acceptance criteria:
1) Microbenchmarks show >=25% CPU reduction on targeted short-prompt traces.
2) End-to-end canary in hosted environment demonstrates 95p latency improvement >=12ms without increased OOMs.
3) No regressions on long-context (>2048) prompt throughput.

Risks and trade-offs:
- Complexity of new allocator increases maintenance cost. Mitigation: keep public API minimal and encapsulate allocator behind runtime adapter.
- SIMD paths must be platform-guarded (fallback slower path). We'll gate with runtime feature-detect and perf flags.
- Eviction tuning could hurt tail workloads with bursty unique prefixes. Mitigation: introduce conservative fallback to LRU when churn exceeds threshold.
comments: 2026-03-02 — Initial design review: PM (Lina Zhou) asked for clear metrics; added acceptance criteria and dashboard items.
2026-03-04 — Spike complete: prototype slab allocator + mock SIMD bridge. Local microbench showed 28% CPU reduction on synthetic short-prompt trace (see /docs/spikes/token-slab/bench-2026-03-04.md).
2026-03-06 — Security/infra sync: confirmed no new network surface; slab data is ephemeral and stored in runtime address space. Security review not required per sec team (ticket SEC-qual note).
2026-03-08 — PR opened for allocator + SIMD bridge (github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4121). Leaving as draft until safe feature-flag gating is in place.

2026-03-10 — Design decision: use frequency-decay eviction (alpha=0.85) with hot-slab bias factor 1.5 for PLG traces. Rationale: preserves tiny common prefixes while allowing memory reclamation for very large unique prompts.
2026-03-11 — Engineering note: added platform guards for AVX512; AVX2 path implemented. Fallback scalar path is 10-15% slower but stable. Need perf matrix on older instance types.
2026-03-12 — QA: integration tests added, still flaky under sustained high-concurrency. Investigating contention in slab allocator; candidate fix: per-thread slab pools.
Review feedback (2026-03-12) — PM Lina: add rollout plan and canary thresholds. Design Ben (runtime lead): measure memory fragmentation and add fragmentation counter to observability.
notes: Next steps: resolve allocator contention (per-thread pools), land guarded PR behind runtime feature flag, run 72h canary in us-west-2 canary pool, and tune decay factor against production sample traces.
